# Enterprise Resolution Intelligence System API v3.5
# Error Resolution Decision Flow

# Error Received

| Yes                | 4xx Error? | No       | 5xx Error?   | No       |
| ------------------ | ---------- | -------- | ------------ | -------- |
| Fix Request        | (Client)   | (Server) | Check Logs & | Escalate |
| Retry with Backoff |            |          |              |          |
# Error/Issue

# 1. Authentication & Authorization Failures

| Code | Error Type         | Cause                               | Solution                                 |
| ---- | ------------------ | ----------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| 401  | Missing Auth       | No API key or token provided        | Include X-API-Key header or Bearer token |
| 401  | Invalid Key        | Malformed or expired API key        | Generate new API key from dashboard      |
| 401  | Token Expired      | JWT or OAuth token expired          | Refresh token or re-authenticate         |
| 403  | Insufficient Scope | API key lacks required permissions  | Request scope upgrade or use correct key |
| 403  | IP Restricted      | Request from unauthorized IP        | Whitelist IP in API settings             |
| 403  | Account Suspended  | Account payment or policy violation | Contact billing or compliance team       |
# Diagnostic Commands:

# Test API key validity
curl -I -H "X-API-Key: your_key" https://api.example.com/v3/auth/validate

# 2. Rate Limiting & Throttling

| Code | Scenario              | Response Headers             | Recovery Action                         |
| ---- | --------------------- | ---------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| 429  | Rate limit exceeded   | X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0     | Wait 60s, implement exponential backoff |
| 429  | Burst limit hit       | X-Burst-Limit-Reset: 1678... | Reduce concurrent requests              |
| 429  | Daily quota exhausted | X-Quota-Remaining: 0         | Upgrade plan or wait 24 hours           |

# Retry Logic Example (Python):

import time

# 3. Input Validation & Request Formatting

| Code | Issue                  | Example Error                   | Fix                             |
| ---- | ---------------------- | ------------------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| 400  | Invalid JSON           | Unexpected token at position 45 | Validate JSON syntax            |
| 400  | Missing required field | Field 'email' is required       | Include all required fields     |
| 422  | Type mismatch          | Expected integer, got string    | Check data types                |
| 422  | Value out of range     | priority must be 1-5            | Use valid value ranges          |
| 422  | Invalid format         | email format invalid            | Match expected format/regex     |
| 413  | Payload too large      | Max size: 5MB                   | Reduce payload or use multipart |

# 4. Server-Side Errors (5xx)

| Code | Error                 | Meaning                        | Action                                           |
| ---- | --------------------- | ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------ |
| 500  | Internal Server Error | Unhandled exception on server  | Retry once; if persists, report with request\_id |
| 502  | Bad Gateway           | Upstream service down          | Retry with exponential backoff (2, 4, 8s)        |
| 503  | Service Unavailable   | Maintenance or overload        | Check status page, retry after 5min              |
| 504  | Gateway Timeout       | Request exceeded timeout (30s) | Optimize query or increase client timeout        |
# 5. Logging & Diagnostic Information

# 5.1 Essential Headers to Log

- X-Request-ID: Unique identifier for tracing (e.g., req_abc123xyz)
- X-Response-Time: Server processing time in milliseconds
- X-RateLimit-*: Rate limit status headers
- Retry-After: Seconds to wait before retrying

# 5.3 What to Log for Debugging

- Full request URL and method
- Request headers (excluding sensitive auth tokens)
- Request body (sanitize PII/credentials)
- Response status code and headers
- Response body (full error object)
- Client timestamp and server timestamp

# 6. Escalation Path

| Error Category    | Self-Service Actions                                      | Escalate If...             | Contact                              |
| ----------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| 4xx Client Errors | * Review docs
* Fix request format
* Check API key scopes | Error persists after fixes | Community forum or developer support |
| Rate Limiting     | - Implement backoff
- Optimize requests
- Cache responses | Need quota increase        | sales\@example.com for plan upgrade  |

# 5xx Server Errors

- Retry 2-3 times
- Check status page with request_id
- Wait 5 minutes

# Auth Issues

- Regenerate API key
- Check IP whitelist
- Verify account status
- Can't generate new key or account suspended

# Critical Production

N/A - immediate escalation

Revenue-impacting outage

# 7. Quick Troubleshooting Checklist

| ✓ | Check          | Action                                     |
| - | -------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| ■ | API Key Valid  | Test with /v3/auth/validate                |
| ■ | Request Format | Validate JSON, check Content-Type header   |
| ■ | Rate Limits    | Check X-RateLimit headers in last response |
| ■ | Network Issues | Test with curl, check DNS resolution       |
| ■ | Logs Captured  | Save request\_id, full request/response    |
| ■ | Status Page    | Visit <https://status.example.com>         |

# API Integration & Authentication Guide

# Enterprise Resolution Intelligence System API v3.5

Base URL: https://api.example.com/v3 Auth: API Key / OAuth 2.0

# 1. Authentication Methods

| Method     | Use Case                                | Implementation                          |
| ---------- | --------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| API Key    | Server-to-server, backend services      | Header: X-API-Key: your\_key            |
| OAuth 2.0  | User-delegated access, web/mobile apps  | Authorization Code / Client Credentials |
| JWT Bearer | Stateless authentication, microservices | Header: Authorization: Bearer \<token>  |

# 1.1 API Key Management

API keys provide simple authentication for server-to-server integrations. Keys are scoped to specific permissions and can be rotated.

# Use API Key in Requests:

curl -H "X-API-Key: sk_live_abc123xyz" https://api.example.com/v3/tickets

- Keys prefixed with sk_live_ (production) or sk_test_ (sandbox)
- Rotate keys every 90 days or immediately if compromised
- Store keys securely in environment variables or secrets manager
# 1.2 OAuth 2.0 Authorization Flow
# 1. Request Auth

# 4. API Response

Client App                  Auth Server                  API Server
# 2. Access Token

# 3. API Request + Token

Client                  OAuth Server                  API Server

# Step 1: Redirect User to Authorization URL

GET https://auth.example.com/oauth/authorize?
client_id=your_client_id&response_type=code&redirect_uri=your_callback

# Token Response:

{ "access_token": "eyJhbG...", "token_type": "Bearer", "expires_in": 3600, "refresh_token": "..." }

# 2. Rate Limiting Rules

| Tier         | Requests/Min | Daily Quota | Burst Limit |
| ------------ | ------------ | ----------- | ----------- |
| Free         | 60           | 10,000      | 100/10s     |
| Basic        | 300          | 100,000     | 500/10s     |
| Professional | 1,200        | 500,000     | 2,000/10s   |
| Enterprise   | Custom       | Unlimited   | Custom      |

# Rate Limit Headers:

- X-RateLimit-Limit: Maximum requests allowed
- X-RateLimit-Remaining: Requests remaining in current window
- X-RateLimit-Reset: Unix timestamp when limit resets

# Handling Rate Limit Exceeded (429):

HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 60
{ "error": "rate_limit_exceeded", "message": "Rate limit exceeded. Retry after 60 seconds" }

# 3. API Error Codes Reference

| Code | Error               | Description                           | Resolution                        |
| ---- | ------------------- | ------------------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| 400  | Bad Request         | Invalid request format or parameters  | Check request body and parameters |
| 401  | Unauthorized        | Missing or invalid authentication     | Provide valid API key or token    |
| 403  | Forbidden           | Insufficient permissions for resource | Check API key scopes              |
| 404  | Not Found           | Resource does not exist               | Verify resource ID                |
| 409  | Conflict            | Resource state conflict               | Retry with updated data           |
| 422  | Validation Error    | Request validation failed             | Fix validation errors in response |
| 429  | Rate Limited        | Too many requests                     | Implement exponential backoff     |
| 500  | Internal Error      | Server-side error                     | Retry or contact support          |
| 502  | Bad Gateway         | Upstream service unavailable          | Retry with exponential backoff    |
| 503  | Service Unavailable | Temporary service outage              | Check status page, retry later    |
# 4. Integration Best Practices

# 4.1 Security

- Never expose API keys in client-side code or version control
- Use HTTPS for all API requests
- Implement token refresh logic for OAuth flows
- Rotate API keys periodically (recommended: every 90 days)

# 4.2 Error Handling

- Always check HTTP status codes before parsing response
- Implement retry logic with exponential backoff for 5xx errors
- Log request_id from error responses for support tickets
- Handle rate limiting gracefully using Retry-After header

# 4.3 Performance

- Use pagination for list endpoints (max 100 items per page)
- Implement request caching to reduce API calls
- Use webhooks for real-time updates instead of polling
- Batch requests when possible to optimize rate limit usage
# 5. Quick Start Code Examples

# cURL Example:

curl -X GET https://api.example.com/v3/tickets \
-H "X-API-Key: sk_live_abc123" \
-H "Content-Type: application/json"

# 6. Key API Endpoints

| Endpoint        | Method | Description              |
| --------------- | ------ | ------------------------ |
| /v3/tickets     | GET    | List all support tickets |
| /v3/tickets     | POST   | Create new ticket        |
| /v3/tickets/:id | GET    | Get ticket details       |
| /v3/tickets/:id | PATCH  | Update ticket            |
| /v3/users       | GET    | List users               |
| /v3/analytics   | GET    | Get analytics data       |
| /v3/webhooks    | POST   | Register webhook         |

ITIL Incident Management Summary
# ITIL 4 Framework for Enterprise Service Management

# 1. Incident Management Overview

Incident Management is the ITIL process responsible for managing the lifecycle of all incidents. The primary objective is to restore normal service operation as quickly as possible while minimizing adverse impact on business operations.

# Key Objectives:

- Restore normal service operation quickly
- Minimize business impact and disruption
- Ensure incidents are resolved within agreed SLA timeframes
- Maintain quality and availability of IT services
- Improve user and customer satisfaction

# 1.1 Incident Lifecycle Stages

| 1. Detection & Recording | 2. Classification & Prioritization | 3. Diagnosis & Investigation | 4. Resolution & Recovery |
| ------------------------ | ---------------------------------- | ---------------------------- | ------------------------ |
| Yes                      | Major                              | 5. Incident Management       | Incident?                |
| (Separate Process)       |                                    |                              |                          |

Knowledge Management

Problem Management

Change Management

Service Request Fulfillment

Supporting ITIL Processes

# 2. Incident Lifecycle Stage Details

| Stage                              | Activities                                                                                              | Key Outputs                                       | Tools/Methods                                                  |
| ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1. Detection & Recording           | * Identify incident source
* Create incident record
* Assign unique ticket ID
* Capture initial details | Incident ticket with:                             | - Timestamp
- Reporter
- Symptoms                              |
| 2. Classification & Prioritization | * Categorize by type
* Assess urgency
* Determine impact
* Calculate priority                           | Priority (P0-P3) based on urgency × impact matrix | - ITSM tool
- Priority matrix
- Service catalog
- SLA database |

# 3. Diagnosis & Investigation

- Gather information
- Identify symptoms
- Check knowledge base
- Investigate root cause

# Diagnosis with:

- Knowledge base
- Probable cause
- Resolution path
- Diagnostic tools
- Error logs
- Known errors

# 4. Resolution & Recovery

- Implement fix
- Test solution
- Restore service
- Confirm with user

# Service restored to normal operation with:

- Change mgmt
- Config mgmt
- Workarounds
- Escalation

# 5. Incident Closure

- Verify resolution
- Update records
- User satisfaction
- Document lessons

# Closed ticket with:

- ITSM closure
- Resolution
- Time metrics
- Feedback
- KB updates
- Trend analysis

# 3. Incident Prioritization

Priority is determined by assessing both the urgency (how quickly resolution is needed) and impact (extent of business disruption) of the incident.

|         | Low    | Medium | High |
| ------- | ------ | ------ | ---- |
| Low     | P3     | P3     | P2   |
| Urgency | P3     | P2     | P1   |
|         | Medium | P2     | P1   |
| High    | P2     | P1     | P0   |

Priority:

- P0: Critical
- P1: High
- P2: Medium
- P3: Low

| Level  | Impact Definition                                                                               | Urgency Definition                                                                  |
| ------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| High   | * Affects multiple users/services
* Critical business function down
* Revenue/compliance impact | - Immediate resolution required
- Business operations stopped
- SLA breach imminent |
| Medium | * Affects single user/department
* Important but not critical
* Workaround available            | - Resolution needed today
- Reduced productivity
- Can wait few hours               |
| Low    | * Minimal business impact
* Cosmetic issues
* Individual convenience                            | - Can be scheduled
- No immediate pressure
- Next business day OK                   |

# 4. Major Incident Management

A Major Incident is the highest category of impact requiring separate procedures and expedited resolution processes.

| Criteria         | Threshold                               | Examples                                                  |
| ---------------- | --------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| User Impact      | > 100 users OR > 25% of user base       | Email system down, network outage, authentication failure |
| Business Impact  | Critical business function unavailable  | E-commerce site down, payment processing halted           |
| Financial Impact | > $50,000/hour revenue loss             | Production system outage, order processing stopped        |
| Duration         | Outage > 4 hours for critical service   | Prolonged degradation of essential services               |
| Security         | Data breach or active security incident | Ransomware, data exfiltration, unauthorized access        |
| Compliance       | Regulatory violation or SLA breach      | GDPR data exposure, contractual SLA failure               |

# 4.1 Major Incident Procedure

- Immediate actions: Convene incident response team, establish war room/bridge
- Communication: Executive notification, status page updates, stakeholder briefings
- Coordination: Incident manager coordinates all technical teams

# 5. Root Cause Analysis (RCA) Requirements

RCA is mandatory for all P0 and P1 incidents, and recommended for recurring P2 incidents. The goal is to identify the underlying cause and prevent recurrence.

| Phase                        | Activities                                                                                   | Deliverables                                             | Timeline                      |
| ---------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| 1. Data Collection           | • Gather logs, metrics • Interview stakeholders • Document timeline • Collect evidence       | Complete incident timeline with all actions and events   | Within 24 hours of resolution |
| 2. Root Cause Identification | • 5 Whys analysis • Fishbone diagram • Fault tree analysis • Identify contributing factors   | Root cause(s) and contributing factors identified        | Within 3 days                 |
| 3. Corrective Actions        | • Define preventive measures • Assign owners • Set implementation dates • Risk assessment    | Action plan with: - Remediation - Prevention - Detection | Within 5 days                 |
| 4. Documentation & Review    | • Write RCA report • Present to stakeholders • Update knowledge base • Share lessons learned | Published RCA report with action tracking                | Within 7 days                 |

# 5.1 RCA Report Structure

- Executive Summary: Impact, duration, business cost, resolution
- Incident Timeline: Chronological sequence of events with timestamps
- Root Cause: Primary cause and contributing factors
- 5 Whys Analysis: Drill-down questioning to find root cause
- Action Items: Short-term fixes and long-term preventive measures
- Lessons Learned: What worked well, what needs improvement
- Follow-up Plan: Action owner assignments with due dates

# 5.2 Key Incident Metrics

| Metric                | Definition                                         | Target                  |
| --------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------- |
| MTTR                  | Mean Time To Resolve (detection to resolution)     | P0: < 4hrs, P1: < 24hrs |
| MTTA                  | Mean Time To Acknowledge (detection to assignment) | P0: < 15min, P1: < 1hr  |
| First Call Resolution | % of incidents resolved on first contact           | > 70%                   |
| Escalation Rate       | % of incidents escalated to L2/L3                  | < 25%                   |
| Reopen Rate           | % of incidents reopened after closure              | < 5%                    |
| SLA Compliance        | % of incidents meeting response/resolution SLAs    | > 95%                   |

Performance & Scalability Guide
Enterprise Resolution Intelligence System API v3.5

# 1. Latency Expectations & SLAs

| Operation           | P50   | P95   | P99   | Notes                              |
| ------------------- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ---------------------------------- |
| GET /tickets (list) | 50ms  | 150ms | 300ms | Cacheable, pagination required     |
| GET /tickets/:id    | 30ms  | 80ms  | 150ms | Single record, cache-friendly      |
| POST /tickets       | 100ms | 250ms | 500ms | Writes to DB, invalidates cache    |
| POST /analytics     | 500ms | 1.5s  | 3s    | Heavy computation, async preferred |
| POST /search        | 200ms | 600ms | 1.2s  | Full-text search, index-dependent  |

# Latency Optimization Tips:

- Use pagination (max 100 items per page) to reduce response size
- Implement field filtering with ?fields=id,status,priority to reduce payload
- Leverage ETags for conditional requests (If-None-Match header)
- Choose nearest region endpoint to minimize network latency

# 2. Throughput & Capacity Limits

| Tier         | Req/Second | Concurrent Connections | Burst Capacity | Payload Limit |
| ------------ | ---------- | ---------------------- | -------------- | ------------- |
| Free         | 5          | 10                     | 20/10s         | 1 MB          |
| Basic        | 50         | 100                    | 100/10s        | 5 MB          |
| Professional | 200        | 500                    | 400/10s        | 10 MB         |
| Enterprise   | 1,000+     | 5,000+                 | Custom         | 50 MB         |

# 3. Caching Strategy & Mechanisms

|                      | 1. Request  | 2b. Cache Miss   |
| -------------------- | ----------- | ---------------- |
| Client               | Cache Layer | Database         |
| 2a. Cache Hit (fast) | Redis/CDN   | 3. Fetch & Cache |

Latency: ~10ms (cache) vs ~100ms (DB)

Cache Hit Ratio Target: >90%

# 3.1 Cache Control Headers

| Header | Value | Use Case |
| ------ | ----- | -------- |
|        |       |          |

# 3.2 Client-Side Caching Example

import requests_cache
session = requests_cache.CachedSession('api_cache', expire_after=300)
response = session.get('https://api.example.com/v3/tickets')

| Cache-Control | public, max-age=300 | Cache for 5 minutes (read-heavy data)     |
| ------------- | ------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| Cache-Control | private, max-age=60 | User-specific data, 1-minute cache        |
| Cache-Control | no-cache            | Always revalidate with server (ETag)      |
| ETag          | "abc123xyz"         | Resource version for conditional requests |
# 4. Scaling Best Practices

# Load Balancer

| Server 1 | Server 2 | Server 3 | Server N |
| -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- |

Horizontal Scaling: Add more servers to handle load

# 4.1 Horizontal vs Vertical Scaling

| Aspect       | Horizontal Scaling         | Vertical Scaling                    |
| ------------ | -------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| Definition   | Add more servers/instances | Increase CPU/RAM of existing server |
| Cost         | Linear cost increase       | Exponential cost at high tier       |
| Availability | High (redundancy)          | Single point of failure             |
| Complexity   | Load balancing required    | Simple architecture                 |
| Limit        | Nearly unlimited           | Hardware ceiling                    |
| Recommended  | ✓ Production systems       | Development/testing                 |

# 4.2 Connection Pooling

Reuse persistent connections to reduce overhead:

# Python example
from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter
session = requests.Session()
adapter = HTTPAdapter(pool_connections=10, pool_maxsize=20, max_retries=3)
session.mount('https://', adapter)
• pool_connections: Number of connection pools to cache
• pool_maxsize: Max connections per pool
• max_retries: Retry failed requests automatically

# 4.3 Async/Batch Operations

- Use /v3/batch endpoint to create multiple tickets in single request (up to 100)
- Leverage webhooks for async notifications instead of polling
- Implement request queuing for non-critical operations
- Use streaming responses for large datasets (Transfer-Encoding: chunked)

# 5. Regional Deployment & Optimization

| Region  | Endpoint                | Avg Latency | Features                  |
| ------- | ----------------------- | ----------- | ------------------------- |
| US East | us-east.api.example.com | 50-150ms    | Primary, full feature set |

# Regional Selection Strategy:

- Auto-routing: Use global endpoint for automatic routing to nearest region
- Manual selection: Pin to specific region for data residency requirements
- Multi-region: Deploy in multiple regions for disaster recovery (Enterprise)
- Latency test: Use /v3/ping endpoint to measure round-trip time

# 6. Performance Monitoring Metrics

| Metric                     | Threshold | Action                              |
| -------------------------- | --------- | ----------------------------------- |
| Response Time (P95)        | > 500ms   | Enable caching, optimize queries    |
| Error Rate                 | > 1%      | Check logs, review recent changes   |
| Cache Hit Ratio            | < 85%     | Increase TTL, review cache strategy |
| Rate Limit Usage           | > 80%     | Implement backoff, upgrade tier     |
| Connection Pool Exhaustion | Frequent  | Increase pool size, check leaks     |
| Timeout Rate               | > 0.1%    | Optimize queries, increase timeout  |

# 7. Quick Optimization Checklist

| ✓ | Optimization                            | Impact                        |
| - | --------------------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| ■ | Enable response compression (gzip)      | 50-70% bandwidth reduction    |
| ■ | Implement client-side caching           | 80-90% reduction in API calls |
| ■ | Use connection pooling                  | 30-40% latency improvement    |
| ■ | Paginate large result sets              | 10x faster response times     |
| ■ | Select nearest region endpoint          | 50-200ms latency reduction    |
| ■ | Use batch endpoints for bulk operations | 90% reduction in requests     |
| ■ | Implement conditional requests (ETags)  | Zero payload on 304 responses |

# Overview

This guide provides comprehensive instructions for installing and configuring the Enterprise Resolution Intelligence System. The installation process covers environment setup, dependency management, configuration, and initial deployment validation.

# Installation Process Flow

| -------------------------- | -- | ------------ | --- | ----------------------- |
# 1. Environment Prerequisites
# 1.1 System Requirements
# 1. System Requirements

# 1.1 Hardware Requirements

| Component | Minimum  | Recommended | Notes                |
| --------- | -------- | ----------- | -------------------- |
| CPU       | 4 cores  | 8+ cores    | x86\_64 architecture |
| RAM       | 8 GB     | 16 GB       | 32 GB for production |
| Storage   | 50 GB    | 200 GB SSD  | Separate data volume |
| Network   | 100 Mbps | 1 Gbps      | Low latency required |

# 1.2 Software Dependencies

| Software         | Version          | Purpose                         |
| ---------------- | ---------------- | ------------------------------- |
| Operating System | Ubuntu 22.04 LTS | Host operating system           |
|                  | CentOS 8+        |                                 |
|                  | RHEL 8+          |                                 |
| Docker           | 20.10+           | Container runtime               |
| Docker Compose   | 2.0+             | Multi-container orchestration   |
| PostgreSQL       | 14.x or 15.x     | Primary database                |
| Redis            | 7.0+             | Caching and session management  |

# 1.3 Network Requirements

- Ports 80 (HTTP) and 443 (HTTPS) must be open for web access
- Port 5432 (PostgreSQL) for database connections

# 2. Deployment Steps

# 2.1 Deployment Architecture

| Load Balancer      | NGINX / HAProxy    |                           |              |
| ------------------ | ------------------ | ------------------------- | ------------ |
| Application Server | Application Server | Background Worker Service |              |
| Node 1 Port: 8080  | Node 2 Port: 8080  | Async Tasks               |              |
| Database           | Cache Layer        | Message Queue             | File Storage |
| PostgreSQL/MySQL   | Redis/Memcached    | RabbitMQ/Kafka            | S3/NFS       |
# 2.2 Step-by-Step Installation

# Step 1: System Preparation

Update system packages and install prerequisites:

sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y
sudo apt install -y curl wget git build-essential

# Step 2: Install Docker

curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com -o get-docker.sh
sudo sh get-docker.sh
sudo usermod -aG docker $USER

# Step 3: Install Docker Compose

sudo curl -L "https://github.com/docker/compose/releases/download/v2.20.0/docker-compose-$(uname -s)-$(uname -m)" -o /usr/local/bin/docker-compose
sudo chmod +x /usr/local/bin/docker-compose

# Step 4: Download Application Package

wget https://releases.example.com/eris-v3.5.tar.gz
tar -xzf eris-v3.5.tar.gz
cd eris-v3.5

# Step 5: Configure Environment Variables

cp .env.example .env
nano .env # Edit configuration

# Step 6: Initialize Database

./scripts/init-database.sh
./scripts/run-migrations.sh

# Step 7: Start Services

docker-compose up -d

# Step 8: Verify Installation

docker-compose ps # Check all services are running
curl http://localhost:8080/health # Health check
# 3. Configuration Setup

# 3.1 Core Configuration Parameters

| Parameter       | Description            | Default    | Required |
| --------------- | ---------------------- | ---------- | -------- |
| DB\_HOST        | Database hostname      | localhost  | Yes      |
| DB\_PORT        | Database port          | 5432       | Yes      |
| DB\_NAME        | Database name          | eris\_prod | Yes      |
| DB\_USER        | Database username      | postgres   | Yes      |
| DB\_PASSWORD    | Database password      | —          | Yes      |
| REDIS\_HOST     | Redis hostname         | localhost  | Yes      |
| REDIS\_PORT     | Redis port             | 6379       | Yes      |
| APP\_PORT       | Application port       | 8080       | No       |
| LOG\_LEVEL      | Logging verbosity      | info       | No       |
| SESSION\_SECRET | Session encryption key | —          | Yes      |
| LICENSE\_KEY    | Product license key    | —          | Yes      |

# 3.2 Security Configuration

- Generate strong session secret: openssl rand -base64 32
- Enable SSL/TLS for production deployments
- Configure firewall rules to restrict database access
- Set up authentication for Redis if exposed

# 4. Common Setup Errors & Solutions

| Error                     | Cause                                | Solution                                                 |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| Port already in use       | Another service using port 8080      | Stop conflicting service or change APP\_PORT in .env     |
| Database connection       | PostgreSQL not running or refused    | Check DB\_\* parameters and ensure PostgreSQL is running |
| Permission denied         | Insufficient file system permissions | Run: sudo chown -R $USER:$USER /opt/eris                 |
| Docker daemon not running | Docker service not started           | Run: sudo systemctl start docker                         |
| Invalid license key       | Expired or malformed license         | Contact support for license renewal                      |
| Out of memory             | Insufficient RAM allocation          | Increase system RAM or adjust Docker memory limits       |
| Migration failed          | Database schema mismatch             | Restore database backup and re-run migrations            |

# 5.1 Operating System Compatibility

| Operating System         | Versions             | Support Status             |

- Credit monitoring: Offer 12-24 months for SSN/financial data breaches

# 6. Post-Incident Review Requirements

Within 5 business days of incident closure, conduct post-mortem including:

- Timeline reconstruction: Complete incident timeline with all actions taken
- Root cause analysis: Technical and procedural factors that enabled incident
- Impact assessment: Systems affected, data exposed, downtime incurred
- Response effectiveness: What worked well, what needs improvement
- Action items: Preventive measures with owners and deadlines
- Documentation: Store in secure incident database for trend analysis

# 4.1 Escalation Path

- Level 1 (L1): Front-line support engineers (initial triage and common issues)
- Level 2 (L2): Senior engineers and specialists (complex troubleshooting)
- Level 3 (L3): Engineering team (product bugs, code fixes)
- Management: Support managers (process issues, SLA breaches)
- Executive: VP of Support or CTO (critical business impact)
# 5. Resolution Ownership & Accountability

# 5.1 Primary Ownership

- Support engineer assigned to ticket maintains ownership until resolution or escalation
- Owner responsible for: investigation, updates, coordination, and final resolution
- Handoffs require explicit acceptance from receiving engineer
- Ownership tracked in ticket system with audit trail

# 5.2 Escalation Ownership

- When escalated, senior engineer assumes primary ownership
- Original engineer remains as secondary contact for context
- Customer always has single point of contact (SPOC)

# 5.3 Resolution Criteria

| Resolution Type  | Criteria                                     | Closure Process                              |
| ---------------- | -------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| Permanent Fix    | Root cause addressed, verified in production | Close after 48-hour monitoring period        |
| Workaround       | Temporary solution, permanent fix planned    | Create follow-up ticket for permanent fix    |
| Configuration    | Settings adjusted, system functioning        | Document changes, close ticket               |
| Cannot Reproduce | Unable to replicate issue after 3 attempts   | Document steps, close with reopen option     |
| By Design        | Behavior is intentional, not a bug           | Explain design rationale, offer alternatives |
